full_judgment: 6. Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mamun, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, seriously opposed the above submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants and contended that this point ought to have been raised before the trial Court in due course and then a report from the trial Court on the calculation of the working days could be obtained therefrom to assess the correctness of the above submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant; but that having not been done and the calculation sheet produced now having not been filed as an Annexure with any verified application by the appellants this should not be taken into consideration and relied upon at this stage. Next, it is the submission of the learned Advocate for the State that even if the calculation sheet as filed in this court is carefully examined, it will be found that the calculation of the working days has been made absolutely on a wrong basis and that some of the days were liable to be excluded from the category of working days, as shown in the calculation sheet but that was not done He further submits that the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants to the effect that the working days being the working days of the court only and not of the concerned Judge the calculation sheet showed that 292 working days already elapsed up to the date of judgment of the case, whereas according to the statute, the trial ought to have been concluded within (240+30) = 270 days i.e. there was a delay of 22 days in the conclusion of the trial as per the decision cited by him in the case of Nayan @ Fazlul Haq Vs. State reported in 38 DLR 415, is wrong and not sustainable in law and facts. Mr. Mamun, the learned AAG, however contends that working days mean the working days of the tria! Judge and not of the court and as such if the concerned Judge is on leave that period of leave must also be excluded in computing the statutory period of the working days for holding the trial of the case. In support of his contention, he has relied on a decision in the case of Abul Kashem and another Vs. State, 40 DLR (AD) 97. He also relied on some other decisions of similar nature reported in 40 DLR at pages 29, 139 and 144. It appears from the order-sheet of the instant case that it was received by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-in-charge Naogaon from the court of the Upazila Magistrate on 14.7.90. It further appears that the concerned Sessions Judge was on leave on that date, hence the learned Additional Sessions Judge-in-charge fixed 21.8.90 as the next date on which date the learned Sessions Judge was present in court and got hold of the case record, but the accused were absent in the court being on bail granted by the Upazila Magistrate. From the order dated 11.2.91 it appears that the learned Sessions Judge was meanwhile transferred and the learned Additional Sessions Judge, was in-charge of the court of the learned Sessions Judge. Of course, on the next date i.e. 27.3.91 the new Sessions Judge joined the court and took over this case for trial and some witnesses were also examined and then 28.3.91 was fixed for further hearing. Thereafter 7.7.91 was fixed for hearing by the learned Additional Sessions Judge. Further it appears from the order sheet that the hearing of the case was concluded on 29.7.91 by the learned Sessions Judge and 4.8.91 was fixed for judgment but on the above date the judgment could not be ready and 11.8.91 was fixed for delivery of the judgment and accordingly the judgment was delivered on the above date. Mr. Abdus Salam Mamun, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, has contended that the period firstly from 14.7.90 to 21.8.90 which was more than a month could not be termed as working days as the judge concerned was on leave and thereafter the learned Sessions Judge was transferred on 11.2.91 and the new Sessions Judge joined his office at Naogaon and took up this case for hearing only on 27.3.91, hence the period starting from 11.2.91 to 27.3.91 could not be calculated as the working days for this case as the concerned Judge was transferred and the new Sessions Judge did not join the station. Similarly, the period from 7.7.91 to 27.7.91 for 20 days, the concerned Judge was on leave as transpired from the order sheet and that period must also be excluded from the period of working days. Thus if proper calculation was done, then the period of working days till the conclusion of the trial would be much less than the statutory period of 270 days and as such the trial was held within time. Mr. Mamun has relied on some decisions, one reported in 38 DLR 233 (ldris Howlader & another Vs. State) and 44 DLR 116 (Husain Muhammad Ershad Vs. State) showing that the conclusion of the trial does not include the delivery of judgment of the case. In the instant case as pointed out, the hearing was concluded on 29.7.91 and the next date was fixed for judgment; so in view of the above decision, the trial in fact was concluded on 29.7.91 but from the calculation sheet as submitted on behalf of the appellants it appears that the learned Advocate for the appellants has also included the period from 29.7.91 to 11.8.91, that means about 13 days as the working days for conclusion of the trial which is not permissible. Thus the contention of the learned AAG was that the calculation of the working days for trial of this case as made out by the learned Advocate for the appellants is wholly wrong and illegal and that the trial of the instant case was concluded within the statutory period and as such it was not hit by section 339C of the Code of Criminal Procedure as amended. We have examined the order sheet of this case and gone through the decisions cited above and considered the submissions made at the bar and we are of the view that the learned Assistant Attorney- General is absolutely correct in his submission on this point and the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants has no substance or legal force. The principle regarding calculation of working days settled in the decision reported in 40 DLR (AD) 97 is very clear on the point urged before us and the same is binding on this court.
